content.text:
All three cases sort correctly. Here's what changed and why:

**`Sortable<T>`** — three-method interface (`size`, `get`, `set`) that captures everything `RadixSorter` needs from a container. Static factory methods `of(T[])` and `of(List<T>)` keep call sites concise; new container types (e.g. a custom ring buffer) just need their own `Sortable` adapter.

**`ArraySortable<T>` / `ListSortable<T>`** — thin package-private adapters. `ListSortable` delegates to `List.get`/`List.set`, which any `ArrayList` or `LinkedList` satisfies. Neither adapter copies data.

**`RadixSorter.sort(Sortable<T>)`** — the sorter no longer knows about arrays or lists. `countSort` accumulates into a plain `Object[]` buffer (same allocation pattern as before), then writes back through `s.set(i, (T) output[i])`. The cast is safe because every value in `output` was put there by `s.get(i)`.

**`main`** demonstrates the two adapters: an `Integer[]` sorted via `ArraySortable`, and a `List<Integer>` / `List<String>` sorted via `ListSortable` — both going through the exact same `RadixSorter` code path.
